title: Bop and Leonard Feather; musicians don't theorize
summary: Rose says bop has no jazz derivation and attacks Leonard Feather's integrity. He says musicians want jobs, not theory, and one pianist told him jazz is whatever a jazz musician plays.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Okay, well, we were talking about Big Spider Beck and you were telling me that he had, he probably would have played bop but would have realized its limitations and gone on to play something else.
Of course. Keep in mind that we're not talking about an area in which I am an expert. We're only talking about my tastes and speculation.
Yeah, but you don't, for instance, when we talk about bop, you certainly wouldn't agree from the way you've defined jazz that bop is in some way a different style of jazz.
Oh, no, no. Bop is not related to jazz in any way. It has no jazz derivation and no jazz sources.
Well, why are musicians unsatisfied to use the word jazz as well as critics like, say, Leonard Feather or something like that?

Well, of course, as far as Leonard Feather is concerned, this man is completely venal and will say or write anything that's going to make him any money. And he has no artistic or personal integrity whatever. And I would welcome nothing more than a libel suit against me for making the statements. And it would be a great pleasure to get him into court and demonstrate all this. So that's not, you can't even consider reasonably Leonard Feather as a person. Musicians, of course, are not interested in theory. Musicians are interested primarily, number one, in jobs. And subsequent to that, given the fact that they have a job of, at some point down the line, trying to find some kind of channel that's going to express their own individual musical personalities.
Yeah, and they're also too busy playing to really think much about it, aren't they?

They are. And besides that, there is nothing in their environment that encourages them to think about it. So they're not, for instance, like French Impressionist painters who would not only paint, but to get together over coffee in the sidewalk cafes and do the intellectual work, abetted by the philosophers of the day, to decide what they were doing. They never lived in that kind of an environment. And, of course, many of them don't have even the kind of formal education to make it possible to communicate on these terms. So you can never think of a jazz musician in terms of his theoretical capacity. And you get some very frustrating reactions from musicians. For instance, one really remarkable jazz piano player, not from New Orleans, but one of the greatest of the jazz piano players, tells me, in the first place, he resents my attitude about the whole thing. You see, in the first place, he says, well, you're not even a musician. How in the hell do you know anything about jazz? And, of course, this is a kind of a representative of a reasonably consistent feeling among many jazz musicians, you see. And he says, you couldn't know anything about jazz because jazz is anything that a jazz musician plays. Now, this is a purely visceral response. And, of course, does nothing at all to help with the understanding of the music. And it is also true that even this man's music would be relatively little understood or appreciated were it not for the people who had been able to identify, recognize, and publicize that which he's doing. But, as a matter of fact, speaking of Feather, Feather is a musician and knows virtually nothing at all about the nature of jazz.
